extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, journalists and public-intelligence practitioners, civic educators
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes W. Lippmann’s conceptual criteria about the nature, function, limits, and proper role of public opinion and democratic institutions — i.e., when publics should act, what counts as valid public judgment, and what institutional supports are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutralization of arbitrary force
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary function of public action is the neutralization of arbitrary force rather than direct administration of complex affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publics should intervene chiefly to check or neutralize concentrations of unchecked power; the public’s role is to produce conditions in which special-purpose agents can make and enforce detailed adjustments. Public action is most effective when it acts to neutralize arbitrary force and then withdraws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agents and bystanders (public vs actors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between those who act (agents who execute and administer affairs) and the public as interested spectators or bystanders who form opinions but do not perform executive acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposals and institutions by whether they respect this division: the public should not be expected to perform executive technical tasks; instead it should express judgments that guide or restrain agents. Systems should make visible who is the actor and who the spectator, and avoid asking the public to carry out what only specialized agents can do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unattainable ideal of the omnicompetent sovereign citizen
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal of an omniscient, omnipotent sovereign citizen competent to decide all public matters is unattainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject reforms premised on citizens’ having time, knowledge, and appetite to master every public problem (e.g., expecting every voter to be fully informed on all technical issues). Design institutions that do not demand omnipresence or omniscience from citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of education as a remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Education cannot realistically teach citizens the facts of every changing public problem; at best it can impart an intellectual attitude or pattern of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing civic-education proposals, prefer those that teach general modes of inquiry and disposition toward problems rather than attempting encyclopedic factual instruction. Beware promises that schooling alone will make the mass competent to govern rapidly changing technical affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of 'more democracy' as a universal cure
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending direct democratic techniques (initiative, referendum, recalls, more frequent voting) presupposes an already competent public and may simply increase bewilderment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess democratic reforms by whether they increase citizens’ effective control or merely increase opportunities to express vague, uninformed opinions; avoid measures that multiply civic tasks beyond the public’s capacity for informed attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of economic/revolutionary remedies (socialist critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transferring more industrial decisions to popular voting or concentrating economic ownership in the state assumes popular technical competence and risks overloading citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate economic-political programs by whether they substitute large-scale, politically-managed tasks for decentralized, detail-sensitive adjustments that require technical administration; favor solutions that create many localized, enforceable rules rather than wholesale political control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific versus general opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific opinions (concrete choices in one’s own sphere) have immediate executive effects; general opinions (public judgments) mainly produce symbolic acts (votes, resolutions) and only indirectly affect administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design processes recognizing that citizens are better at making particular, narrow choices they live with than at continuously directing general policy; use mechanisms that channel specific expertise for implementation rather than expecting general public command of details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a general will: role of symbols and leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders make a homogeneous public will out of heterogeneous desires by assembling emotions through symbols; the process intensifies feeling and degrades significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging political appeals, account for the emotional-symbolic mechanisms that simplify and mobilize publics. Recognize the risk that such processes can replace critical, fact-based judgment with intensified feeling and oversimplified alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of public debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Public debate has value but its chief usefulness is limited: it helps clarify and test alternatives but cannot substitute for detailed fact-finding or technical administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support debate that illuminates choices and exposes maladjustments, but pair it with institutional fact-finding and expert analysis; avoid treating debate alone as sufficient for technically complex decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity and the need for fact‑finding agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern administration requires extensive fact-finding and public accounting; publicity is necessary but primarily serves specialized readers (officials, experts), not every voter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutionalize large-scale fact-finding agencies and public accounting mechanisms; evaluate information-disclosure policies on whether they make complex data usable by decision-makers and intermediaries rather than assuming mass absorption by all citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests of rules and laws (defective rule, inquiry, conformity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and laws should be evaluated by definable tests (e.g., conformity test, inquiry test, validity/assent), and defective rules are those that fail these practical tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging legal or institutional rules, apply pragmatic tests: can the rule be understood and followed? does inquiry reveal it to be workable? does its enforcement produce intended behavior? Prefer reforms that pass such operational tests rather than abstract moral assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assent and validity of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The legitimacy of laws involves assent and public understanding; assent is a concept distinct from mere formal enactment and affects the efficacy of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate legislation not only for formal passage but for the degree to which it secures meaningful assent and is intelligible and enforceable in practice; avoid relying on ritualized assent as proof of effective public support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economize public attention (reserve force in crises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because citizens have limited time and attention, the public’s efforts should be economized: the public should keep a reserve of attention to be applied in crises or maladjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design civic responsibilities and institutional prompts that use the public’s attention sparingly and strategically — calling the public into action when neutralization of arbitrary force or major maladjustment is required, not for routine administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many detailed balances of power (pluralist remedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: To control arbitrary power, create many detailed, local balances of power rather than rely on a single, centralized countervailing power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor institutional arrangements that enable different groups affected by an arbitrary power to check and balance it in detail (factory-level, market-specific, local adjudication) instead of seeking wholesale national-level countervailing measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realms of disorder: industrial and international anarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal modern realms of disorder are industrial relations and international affairs where precedents and settled law are scarce and power is anarchic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reforms for these realms by whether they create stable procedures, precedents, and localized adjudicatory mechanisms to transform arbitrary power into settled rules; international disputes often require disassociation of private interests from national advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and principles of public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion should be understood as the voice of interested spectators; its principles include limitation to the public’s competence, economy of attention, and acting to facilitate special-purpose adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these principles as evaluative criteria for institutional design: does a proposed mechanism respect the spectator-character of publics, economize their attention, and assist rather than usurp the work of specialized agents?
